whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Strategy Designer exam for?

personas.label: UX strategists and service designers
personas.description: You run research and design work on Salesforce projects and want a credential that shows it.

personas.label: Consultants leading discovery workshops
personas.description: You lead discovery with clients and turn what you learn into a clear direction for the solution.

personas.label: Product owners bridging design and business
personas.description: You need to connect user needs to business goals and help teams decide what to build first.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Strategy Designer Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: It is a moderate exam, but it isn't about Salesforce features. It tests how you research users, frame the right problem, run workshops and connect design work to business value. People from a pure admin or developer background often find it unfamiliar.
bullets: 70% to pass, per Salesforce's Trailhead prep module. That is 42 correct answers.
Method focus. Research, synthesis, problem framing, facilitation and measuring value.
Judgement questions. Many questions ask what you should do next in a project, not what a tool does.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: People who have run discovery and research on real projects do best. Before you book. Aim for 80% or more on practice tests, since the pass mark is higher than most.

examFormat.heading: Strategy Designer Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions describe a moment in a project, such as a vague client request, conflicting stakeholders or research results that don't match the brief, and ask what the designer should do.
bestWayToPass: Know your research methods: Interviews, observation, surveys and analytics, and when each fits.
Practise synthesis: Affinity mapping, personas, journey maps and service blueprints.
Frame problems well: Turn findings into clear problem statements and How Might We questions.
Tie work to value: Link design decisions to business goals and measures of success.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests how you shape the direction of a Salesforce solution through research, problem framing, facilitation and business value, before and during design.

keyConcepts.h2: Strategy Designer: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Human-Centered Design Strategy
blocks.body: Human-centred design starts with the people who will use a solution. Before suggesting features. Learn about their goals, tasks and frustrations. **Research methods** include interviews, watching people at work (contextual inquiry), surveys and looking at usage data. Pick the method that fits the question: interviews and observation for why people do things, surveys and data for how many. Plan research with a clear goal, recruit the right participants, and avoid leading questions.

blocks.heading: Service Design and Journey Mapping
blocks.body: After research comes **synthesis**: making sense of what you learned. **Affinity mapping** groups notes into themes. **Personas** summarise types of users and their needs. **Journey maps** show the steps a person goes through, what they feel and where it goes wrong. **Service blueprints** add what happens behind the scenes: the staff, systems and processes that support each step. These tools help teams see the whole experience, not just one screen.

blocks.heading: Business Value Framing
blocks.body: Good design has to make sense for the business too. Link each proposed change to a **business goal**, such as faster case resolution or higher conversion, and agree how success will be measured. Map **stakeholders** and understand what each cares about. Use simple prioritisation, like value versus effort, to decide what to do first. A clear **experience vision** gives everyone a shared picture of where the solution is heading and why.

blocks.heading: Agile UX: Design Sprints and Dual-Track
blocks.body: Design work fits into agile delivery. **Design sprints** take a team from problem to tested prototype in a few days. In **dual-track** agile, a discovery track explores and tests ideas while a delivery track builds what has been validated. **Prototypes** can be rough sketches or clickable mock-ups, as long as they let you test ideas with users early. Testing early saves time, because changing a sketch is much cheaper than changing built software.

blocks.heading: Ethics, Inclusion, and Responsible Design
blocks.body: Design choices affect people, so think about who might be left out or harmed. **Inclusive design** means involving a wide range of users, including people with disabilities, and following accessibility standards. Be open about how data is collected and used. Watch for bias in research, such as only talking to the easiest users to reach. With AI features. Think about trust, transparency and what happens when the AI gets it wrong.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Strategy Designer Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions ask what to do next. The right answer usually moves the team toward a better understanding of the problem before jumping to a solution.

blocks.heading: Design Thinking Process
blocks.body: Understand, define, ideate, prototype and test. It is a loop, so going back to research is often the right move.

blocks.heading: Research Methods
blocks.body: Interviews and observation for why. Surveys and analytics for how many. Pick the method that fits the question.

blocks.heading: Journey Mapping
blocks.body: Map the steps, feelings and pain points. Add a service blueprint to show the people and systems behind each step.

blocks.heading: Problem Framing & HMW Statements
blocks.body: Turn findings into a clear problem statement, then How Might We questions that open up ideas without fixing a solution.

blocks.heading: Facilitation Techniques
blocks.body: Plan workshop goals and activities, give everyone a voice, and end with clear decisions and next steps.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Designer Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: Good next steps after Platform Strategy Designer:

sampleQuestions.question: A client asks for a new dashboard because 'sales reps aren't hitting targets'. What should the strategy designer do first?
options: Ask the development team which option would be easiest for them to build
Build the dashboard straight away
Research why reps are missing targets before agreeing on a solution
Copy a dashboard from another client
sampleQuestions.explanation: The request is a solution. Research shows whether a dashboard would actually solve the real problem.
whyWrong: Ease of build doesn't tell you what users need.
Building first risks solving the wrong problem.
Another client's context is different.

sampleQuestions.question: The team needs to understand why service agents keep switching between screens during calls. Which research method fits best?
options: Looking closely at the org's current user licence count
A competitor review
Watching agents at work (contextual inquiry)
A large online survey
sampleQuestions.explanation: Observing agents in their real setting shows what they actually do and why.
whyWrong: Licence count says nothing about behaviour.
Competitors don't explain your agents' behaviour.
Surveys tell you how many, but miss the detail of how and why.

sampleQuestions.question: After 15 interviews, the team has hundreds of sticky notes. What should they do next?
options: Group the notes into themes with affinity mapping
Start building features from the first note
Throw away any research notes that do not match the original brief
Run 15 more interviews straight away
sampleQuestions.explanation: Affinity mapping turns raw notes into themes the team can act on.
whyWrong: Acting on one note ignores the bigger picture.
Discarding inconvenient notes adds bias.
More interviews before synthesis just adds more notes.

sampleQuestions.question: Which artefact shows the steps a customer takes, how they feel at each step, and where problems happen?
options: A data model diagram
A journey map
A release schedule
A test plan
sampleQuestions.explanation: Journey maps show steps, emotions and pain points across an experience.
whyWrong: A data model shows objects and fields.
A release schedule shows delivery dates.
A test plan lists tests.

sampleQuestions.question: The team wants to show both the customer's steps and the staff, systems and processes behind each step. What should they create?
options: A service blueprint
A mood board of visual references
A persona
A wireframe
sampleQuestions.explanation: Service blueprints add the behind-the-scenes layers to a journey.
whyWrong: A mood board shows visual style.
A persona describes a type of user.
A wireframe shows one screen's layout.

sampleQuestions.question: Which is the best example of a How Might We question?
options: Why are agents so slow?
How might we help new agents find answers without asking a colleague?
How might we build a new Lightning page?
Can we go ahead and add three more fields onto the existing case page layout?
sampleQuestions.explanation: A good How Might We question frames the need and leaves room for many ideas.
whyWrong: It blames users and doesn't open up ideas.
It names a solution, not a need.
It is a yes or no question about a specific change.

sampleQuestions.question: Two senior stakeholders want opposite things from the project. What should the strategy designer do?
options: Simply do whatever the louder of the two stakeholders happens to want
Bring them together around shared goals and the research findings
Build both versions
Ignore both and decide alone
sampleQuestions.explanation: Aligning stakeholders on goals and evidence helps reach a decision both can support.
whyWrong: Following the loudest voice ignores evidence.
Building both wastes effort.
Deciding alone loses support for the project.

sampleQuestions.question: The team has 20 ideas and time for 5. How should they choose?
options: Pick the most technically complex
Pick the first five suggested
Pick out whichever of the ideas the project team finds the most fun
Prioritise by value to users and the business against effort
sampleQuestions.explanation: A value versus effort view helps pick the ideas with the best return.
whyWrong: Complexity isn't a goal.
Order of suggestion is random.
Fun doesn't mean valuable.

sampleQuestions.question: The team wants to test a new case flow idea with agents next week, before any building. What should they make?
options: A release note
A full production build of the proposed solution
A simple prototype to test with real agents
A 50-page specification
sampleQuestions.explanation: Early prototypes let you learn from users quickly and cheaply.
whyWrong: Release notes come after building.
A full build is slow and costly to change.
A long spec can't be tested with users.

sampleQuestions.question: In dual-track agile, what does the discovery track do?
options: Explores and tests ideas so the delivery track builds validated work
Runs only right at the very end of the whole delivery project, after build
Writes all the code
Handles production support
sampleQuestions.explanation: Discovery runs alongside delivery, testing ideas before they are built.
whyWrong: Discovery runs throughout, not just at the end.
Delivery writes the code.
Support is separate.

sampleQuestions.question: How should the team show that a redesign was worth it?
options: Ask each of the members of the project team whether they personally like the result
Agree success measures linked to business goals before launch, then track them
Measure how long the project took
Count the number of new screens
sampleQuestions.explanation: Measures tied to goals, set before launch, show whether the change made a difference.
whyWrong: The team's opinion isn't evidence of impact.
Project length doesn't measure value.
Screen count isn't value.

sampleQuestions.question: Research so far has only included office staff, but the solution will also be used by field workers. What is the risk?
options: There is no risk
The project will cost less
The design may not meet field workers' needs because they weren't included
Field workers will eventually adapt themselves to almost anything they are given
sampleQuestions.explanation: Leaving out a user group is a common bias that leads to designs that don't work for them.
whyWrong: Missing a key group is a real risk.
Cost isn't the issue here.
Assuming people will adapt usually fails.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the main purpose of an experience vision?
options: To replace research
To list out every single field that appears on each and every one of the pages
To set the project budget
To give everyone a shared picture of the future experience and why it matters
sampleQuestions.explanation: An experience vision aligns the team and stakeholders on direction.
whyWrong: A vision comes from research, it doesn't replace it.
Field lists are detailed design.
Budget is set separately.

sampleQuestions.question: A workshop with 12 stakeholders keeps being dominated by two people. What should the facilitator do?
options: Use activities like silent idea writing so everyone contributes
Remove the quieter people
Let the two people involved simply carry on exactly as they are now
End the workshop early
sampleQuestions.explanation: Structured activities give everyone a voice and reduce the effect of dominant people.
whyWrong: Removing people is the opposite of the goal.
Letting it continue loses everyone else's input.
Ending early wastes the session.

sampleQuestions.question: A new AI feature will suggest replies to customers. What should the strategy designer consider?
options: Nothing, because AI is always right
Only how fast it runs
Only the background colour of the on-screen suggestion box
Trust and transparency, and what happens when the AI gets it wrong
sampleQuestions.explanation: Responsible design for AI includes clear disclosure, human oversight and handling mistakes.
whyWrong: AI can be wrong, so plan for it.
Speed matters but isn't the main concern.
Visual style is a detail.
